# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is heavy. This single fact explains almost everything about how municipal water systems are designed. A cubic foot of water weighs about 62.4 pounds, and a column of water one foot tall exerts about 0.433 pounds per square inch (psi) of pressure at its base. Engineers call this relationship "head"—the pressure exerted purely by elevation. Understanding head is the key to understanding why your shower works on the twentieth floor.

## The Fundamental Physics: Elevation Head

Imagine a reservoir sitting on a hill 200 feet above a city. Gravity alone gives that water about 87 psi of pressure at the bottom of the hill (200 × 0.433). That's substantial—most household plumbing is designed to operate between 40 and 80 psi. So in principle, if your city sits below its reservoir, gravity does all the work. This is why ancient Roman aqueducts worked without a single pump: engineers maintained a continuous, gentle downhill slope from mountain springs to city fountains, and elevation did the rest.
